title: How to recover a lost paragraph in Google Docs on Mac: version history steps
metaTitle: How to recover a lost paragraph in Google Docs on Mac
description: Lost a paragraph after editing in Google Docs? Use version history on your Mac to get it back, then stop it happening again.
targetKeyword: how to recover a lost paragraph in Google Docs
secondaryKeywords: Google Docs version history on Mac
restore deleted text in Google Docs
recover lost text in Pages on Mac
recover lost text in Word on Mac
intro: To recover a lost paragraph in Google Docs on Mac, open the document and click Last edit at the top right. Pick a version from before the edit, then copy it into a new file or restore it. This page covers the steps, the limits of version history, and the habits that stop it happening again.
tldr: Open Last edit at the top right, then scroll the earlier versions until your paragraph appears.
Copy the version into a new file if you want to keep your current draft exactly as it is.
Google Docs needs edit permission to browse earlier versions. Ask the owner for access if you cannot see them.
Pages and Word on Mac use their own steps. Time Machine can restore local files that it has backed up.
Name versions before big edits, so the one you need is easy to find later.

blocks.text: Recover the paragraph in Google Docs on Mac

Start in the document, not in a backup. Open the file in your browser. Look at the top right corner, then click Last edit. A panel opens on the right with earlier versions. Each version has a date and time, so you can find the one from before your cut. Scroll the list and click a version to view it on screen.

Read the version before you decide. Look for your paragraph, then check the timestamp against the time of your cut. If the text is there, you have the right version. If it is not, scroll to an older version and check again. Do not restore the first version you open without reading it.
Restore or copy the earlier version

items: Restore the earlier version to make it the current version. This brings back the whole document as it was, not just one paragraph.
Copy the earlier version into a new file if you want to keep your current draft untouched. Google Docs lets you do this from version history.
Compare the copy with your current draft. Check dates, headings, and the paragraph before you delete anything.
Paste the recovered paragraph back into the draft by hand if you only need that section.

blocks.text: When you cannot see the version history

Check your permission first. Google says you need edit permission to browse earlier versions. A viewer may see the document but not its history. Ask the owner for edit access, or ask someone with edit access to copy the version and send you the paragraph.
Worked example: a paragraph cut in the morning

Say you cut a paragraph from a Google Doc in the morning. You notice the gap after lunch. Open Last edit and scroll back past the time of the cut. Pick the version from just before it. Check that the paragraph is there, then copy that version into a new file.

Copy the paragraph from the new file and paste it into your current draft at the right spot. Check it against the text around it, because that text may have changed since the morning. Close the copy when you are done, so you do not edit the wrong file.
Recover text in Pages on Mac

Pages keeps its own version history. Open the document, then choose File > Revert To > Browse All Versions. Pick the version with your paragraph. Click Restore to make it current. Hold Option and click Restore a Copy to open it as a separate window, so your current draft stays open.

Apple's Mac help says many apps save versions as you work. The Browse All Versions view can restore a version, restore a copy, delete a version, or leave the document unchanged. Use the copy option when you are not sure. It keeps both versions side by side.
Recover text in Word on Mac

Word depends on where the file lives. Microsoft says you must store a Word document in OneDrive or a SharePoint library to use versioning. A file saved to a local folder does not get AutoSave. A cut in a local draft may therefore have no saved version at all.
Microsoft's versioning page does not give a Mac menu path for version history. Use the version list the app shows you. Check Microsoft's help if the menu looks different on your copy of Word.
Turn on AutoSave in Word

items: Move the draft into OneDrive or a SharePoint library.
Open the file from the File menu inside Word. On Mac, Microsoft says AutoSave does not start otherwise.
Check the AutoSave switch. To change the default, choose Word > Preferences > Save.
Repeat the check in Excel and PowerPoint, because the setting must be changed in each Office app.

blocks.text: If AutoSave is off, changes reach the shared file only after a manual save. AutoRecover still protects against crashes. It does not make every edit reach the file. Save by hand before a risky cut if AutoSave is off.

blocks.title: Test before you trust it
blocks.text: Make a small change in a scratch file, wait a few minutes, then open the history. If the change is missing, the app has not saved a version yet. Learn that gap now, not after you lose a draft.
Use Time Machine for local files

A Pages or Word file on your Mac disk may sit in a Time Machine backup. Open a window for the file's folder. Use Spotlight to open Time Machine, then move back through the backups with the arrows and timeline. Select the file and click Restore.

Restored items return to their original location. That can overwrite a newer copy, so check the file name and date first. Apple's page does not say how often Time Machine makes a backup, so do not assume the last hour is covered.
Google Docs files live in Google's cloud, not on your disk. Time Machine usually has no copy of them. For those files, version history is your main route.
Where each app keeps the earlier text

rows: Last edit at the top right, then the version list
Needs edit permission. Up to 40 named versions. Revisions may occasionally be merged.
File > Revert To > Browse All Versions
Saves a version on each save and every hour. Timing is approximate.
Version list in a file stored on OneDrive or SharePoint
Local folders get no AutoSave. Microsoft gives no Mac menu path.
Apple does not state how often backups run.

blocks.text: Name versions before big edits

Google Docs lets you name a version so it stays easy to find. Open the version history, then choose More > Name this version. A named version is kept from merging with others. Each document can hold 40 named versions, so save names for the versions that matter.

Name the version before you cut, rewrite, or reorder a section. Use a plain label, such as Before cutting the methods section. Later, you search for one name instead of scrolling through every version. That habit makes a restore a short job.
What lost text costs you

Time is the first cost. Rebuilding a paragraph takes effort, and rebuilt text often reads worse than the first draft. The BLS puts median pay for writers and authors at $36.98 an hour for May 2025. At that median, 30 minutes of recreating text costs about $18.
Treat that number as a rough guide. It uses a median wage, not your rate. Work out your own cost by multiplying the minutes you spent rebuilding by your hourly rate, then dividing by 60.
Mistakes people make

items: Relying on undo for an edit you made earlier in the day. Undo covers recent steps only.
Restoring a whole old version when you only needed one paragraph.
Assuming a Word file has AutoSave because it sits on the desktop.
Forgetting that a viewer cannot browse version history in Google Docs.
Deleting version history to tidy up, which Google says is permanent.
Skipping the test, so you learn about the save gap only after a loss.

blocks.text: Edge cases worth knowing

Merged revisions can confuse you. Google says revisions may occasionally be merged. If a version looks wrong, copy it into a new file, check the text, then decide. Named versions help you keep the one you need.
If you pasted a paragraph from another file, search that file's history too. Its earlier text may still be there, even when the current draft lost it.
Shared files add one more question. Anyone with edit permission can make changes, so the history may show edits from more than one person. Check the timestamps before you decide who made a cut.
Privacy and client material

When the paragraph holds private material, check before you share it. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

If your draft holds client or patient data, follow your employer's rules first. Lawyers, nurses, and accountants often have strict rules on this. Ask your employer which tools are approved before you paste anything into an AI app.
Where Lazur helps, honestly

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It does not click buttons, edit files, or restore a version for you. You still do the restore. Lazur shows you where things are and walks you through the steps.
What to ask Lazur during a restore

Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask where Last edit is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Then ask Lazur to guide you through copying an earlier version. It moves one click at a time and waits for each click, so you stay in control.

Once the paragraph is back, hold fn to dictate any rewrite at the cursor. Dictation types clean, formatted text in any app. Dictation is unlimited on Pro and Power, so long rewrites do not use up AI actions.
Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. The [pricing page](/pricing) shows the plans and the trial. You can start a trial without a credit card.
Week plan that keeps paragraphs safe
A short routine beats a long rescue. The plan below takes little time each day. Each step makes the next restore faster, and each one fits a Mac you already use.

blocks.title: Do not rely on one copy
blocks.text: A version history is not a backup. Google says deleting version history is permanent. Keep a second copy of important drafts, such as an export or a Time Machine backup for local files.
Next steps

Start with the Last edit panel today. If the paragraph is there, copy that version into a new file and paste the text back. If it is not, check your Pages or Word backups, and see whether Time Machine holds a copy. For more Google Docs steps, read [Google Docs for writers on Mac](/for/writers/google-docs). For Pages and Word, see [Pages for writers on Mac](/for/writers/pages) and [Word for writers on Mac](/for/writers/word).

faq.question: Can I recover a paragraph I deleted yesterday in Google Docs?
faq.answer: Possibly. Click Last edit at the top right and check versions from before the deletion. If no version from that time appears, version history cannot help, so check your clipboard and any notes you made.

faq.question: Does undo work for a deleted paragraph in Google Docs?
faq.answer: Yes, press ⌘Z right after the loss, while the change is still fresh. Undo covers recent steps only. For an edit from earlier, use version history instead.

faq.question: Why does my version history show so few versions?
faq.answer: Versions are created at set points, not on every keystroke. Edits made between those points may not have their own version. Naming a version before a big change gives you a fixed point to return to.

faq.question: Can I restore a Google Docs version without edit access?
faq.answer: No. Google says you need edit permission to browse earlier versions. Ask the owner for access, or ask someone with edit access to copy the version for you.

faq.question: Is Pages' Browse All Versions the same as Google Docs version history?
faq.answer: No. They are separate apps with separate rules. Pages offers Restore and Restore a Copy in Browse All Versions. Google Docs offers restore and copy into a new file from the Last edit panel.

faq.question: Does Lazur restore my document for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It can show you where Last edit is, then guide you one click at a time while you do the restore.

faq.question: Does Word on Mac save my changes automatically?
faq.answer: Only when the file is saved to OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, or SharePoint Online, and AutoSave is on. A file in a local folder does not get AutoSave, so save it by hand.

faq.question: Is it safe to ask Lazur about a draft with private material?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you and are not stored. If the draft holds client or patient data, follow your employer's rules first.

costs.title: Rebuilding the text takes time
costs.text: A lost paragraph costs time, and rebuilt text often reads worse than the first draft. The BLS puts median pay for writers and authors at $36.98 an hour for May 2025. At that median, 30 minutes of recreating text costs about $18. That is a median wage, not your rate, so use your own number when you check the math.

costs.title: Deadlines can slip
costs.text: A lost section can push back a deadline, especially when an editor or client expects a set draft on a set day. No study measures how often this happens to writers. Treat the risk as real but unmeasured, and plan for it with a copy of each draft.

costs.title: Lost data is common
costs.text: A 2024 Backblaze and Harris Poll survey of 2,058 US adults found that 74% of computer owners had accidentally deleted important data. That survey covers all kinds of data, not writing. It still shows that accidents happen to most people who own a computer.

costs.title: Recovery is not guaranteed
costs.text: In a 2024 Backblaze survey of 300 US IT decision makers, only 42% of organizations that lost data could restore all of it. Businesses are not writers, and the survey is not about text edits. It still shows that a backup does not guarantee a full recovery.

costs.title: Stress and trust with editors
costs.text: Losing work can slow down the next draft, and it can wear down trust with editors who expect clean files. No source measures this for writers. A routine that keeps a copy before risky edits turns a lost paragraph into a short fix.

causes.title: Versions are saved at set points
causes.text: Version history does not record every keystroke. Apple's macOS help says a version is saved every hour, or more often during heavy editing. It also saves when you open, save, duplicate, lock, rename, or revert a document. A cut made between those points may never get its own version. Pages makes a version each time you save, so an edit that never reached a save may not appear in its list.

causes.title: Selecting and typing over text
causes.text: Most lost paragraphs come from a selection. You highlight a paragraph, then type or paste. One keystroke replaces the whole block. Once the document saves, the old wording is no longer in the current draft. Undo can reverse that change, but only while the steps are still available to it.

causes.title: Local Word files have no AutoSave
causes.text: Microsoft says AutoSave turns on only when a file is saved to OneDrive, OneDrive for Business, or SharePoint Online. A file saved to a local folder gets no AutoSave, and versioning also needs OneDrive or SharePoint. On a Mac, AutoSave needs the file opened from Word's File menu. Without AutoSave, changes reach the file only after a manual save.

causes.title: Undo has limits
causes.text: Undo is the fastest tool, and it is the first thing to try. Still, undo covers only the most recent steps. If you made many edits after the cut, undo may not reach back far enough. Version history is the next step, not a second try at undo.

causes.title: Merged revisions in Google Docs
causes.text: Google says revisions may occasionally be merged. If you expect one version and see another, a merge may be the reason. Name important versions to keep them separate from others. Google also says that deleting version history is permanent and cannot be undone.

causes.title: Local files and cloud files are stored differently
causes.text: A local Pages or Word file lives on your Mac disk, so Time Machine can restore it if a backup exists. Google Docs files live in Google's cloud, so a local backup usually does not hold them. Knowing where a file lives tells you which recovery tool to try first.

fixes.title: Try undo first, while the loss is fresh
fixes.text: Press ⌘Z right after the loss, before you do anything else. Press ⇧⌘Z to redo if undo goes too far. Undo covers recent steps only, so move to version history if the paragraph disappeared after more work.

fixes.title: Open Last edit and copy the version
fixes.text: Click Last edit at the top right of the Google Doc. Scroll the list until you find a version with the paragraph. Copy that version into a new file so the current draft stays as it is. Then copy the paragraph back. This is the safest route for Google Docs.

fixes.title: Name versions before big changes
fixes.text: Choose More > Name this version in the version history. Named versions are kept from merging with others. A document can hold 40 named versions, so name the ones that matter and skip the small saves.

fixes.title: Use Browse All Versions in Pages
fixes.text: Choose File > Revert To > Browse All Versions. Pick the version with your paragraph. Hold Option and click Restore a Copy to open it in a separate window, or click Restore to make it current. The same view lets you delete a version or leave the document unchanged.

fixes.title: Turn on AutoSave for Word drafts
fixes.text: Move the draft into OneDrive or a SharePoint library. Open it from Word's File menu. Check the AutoSave setting. To change the default, go to Word > Preferences > Save. Repeat the check in each Office app, because the setting is per app.

fixes.title: Restore a local file with Time Machine
fixes.text: Open a window for the file's folder. Use Spotlight to open Time Machine. Browse with the arrows and timeline until the file appears, select it, and click Restore. Restored items return to their original location, so check that you will not overwrite a newer file by accident.

fixes.title: Keep a scratch file for cut text
fixes.text: Before a risky edit, select the paragraph and press ⌘C. Paste it into a scratch document named Cut scraps. The clipboard holds only the last copy, so the scratch file keeps more than one cut. Clear it once the draft is final.

fixes.title: Test how often your app saves
fixes.text: Make a small change in a scratch document. Wait a few minutes, then open the history. If the change has no version yet, the app saves on a schedule or at set events. Knowing that helps you decide when to name a version by hand.

fixes.title: Check your access before you panic
fixes.text: If you cannot see Last edit or the history panel, check your access. Google needs edit permission to browse earlier versions. Ask the owner for edit access, or ask someone with edit access to copy the version for you.

plan.label: Now
plan.title: Check Last edit before anything else
plan.text: Open the document and click Last edit at the top right. Scroll the versions until your paragraph appears. Copy that version into a new file, then paste the paragraph back into the draft you are working on.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Name the versions you care about
plan.text: Before a cut, rewrite, or reorder, choose More > Name this version. Use a plain name, such as Before cutting the methods section. Named versions are kept from merging with others.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set up AutoSave for Word files
plan.text: Move any Word draft that matters into OneDrive or a SharePoint library. Open it from Word's File menu. Check that AutoSave is on, and check Word > Preferences > Save in each Office app.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Test how your app saves
plan.text: Make a small change in a scratch Pages or Google Docs file. Wait a few minutes, then open Browse All Versions or Last edit. Note whether the change has its own version, so you know how far back a restore can reach.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Check Time Machine for local files
plan.text: Open the folder that holds a local Pages or Word file. Use Spotlight to open Time Machine, then browse to see whether an older copy exists. If nothing shows up, your backup may not cover that folder.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Keep a scratch file for cut text
plan.text: Create a scratch document named Cut scraps. Before a risky edit, select the paragraph, press ⌘C, and paste it into that file. Clear the scratch file once the draft is final.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Set a weekly reminder
plan.text: Ask Lazur to set an Apple Reminders reminder for Friday afternoon. Use it to name a version and to check that your backups still run. Lazur sets the reminder. You still do the checks.
